content: The anatomy of fish is primarily influenced by the physical properties of water, which is significantly denser than air, contains a relatively small amount of dissolved oxygen, and absorbs light more effectively than air. Fish exhibit a wide variety of body plans. Their bodies are generally divided into three regions: the head, trunk, and tail, although these divisions are not always externally visible. Many fish have a fusiform body shape, which is streamlined and common in fast-swimming species. Other body shapes include filiform (eel-like) and vermiform (worm-like). Fish bodies are often laterally compressed (thin) or vertically depressed (flat). The caudal peduncle is the narrow part of the body where the caudal (tail) fin is attached. The hypural joint connects the caudal fin to the last vertebrae, and the hypural structure is often fan-shaped. Some fish possess photophores, which are light-emitting organs that appear as luminous spots. The light can be produced through compounds derived from prey digestion, specialized mitochondrial cells called photocytes, or symbiotic bacteria. These photophores are used for attracting prey or confusing predators. The lateral line is a sensory organ that detects movement and vibrations in the surrounding water. It typically consists of a line of receptors running along each side of the fish. Sharks have specialized structures called ampullae of Lorenzini, which allow them to sense electrical discharges. The genital papilla is a small, fleshy tube located behind the anus in some fish, through which sperm or eggs are released. The shape of the papilla often helps determine the sex of the fish. The head of a fish includes the snout (from the eye to the forward-most point of the upper jaw), the operculum or gill cover (absent in sharks), and the cheek (extending from the eye to the preopercle). The operculum and preopercle may or may not have spines. The lower jaw defines the chin. In lampreys, the mouth is formed into an oral disk, while in most jawed fish, the mouth can be terminal (at the forward end of the head), superior (upturned), or subterminal/inferior (downturned or on the underside of the fish). Some fish have sucker-like mouths adapted for clinging to objects in fast-moving water. The head may also feature fleshy structures called barbels, which can be long and whisker-like. Many fish species have various protrusions or spines on their heads. The nostrils (nares) of most fish do not connect to the oral cavity but are instead pits of varying shapes and depths. Fins are one of the most distinctive features of fish. In bony fish, fins may contain spines or rays. A fin can consist of only spiny rays, only soft rays, or a combination of both. Spiny rays are generally stiff and sharp, while soft rays are flexible, segmented, and may be branched. The segmentation of rays distinguishes them from spines, which are never segmented. The caudal fin, or tail fin, is attached to the end of the caudal peduncle. It can take various forms: Heterocercal tails have vertebrae extending into a larger lobe, making the tail asymmetrical. Epicercal tails have a longer upper lobe (e.g., sharks). Hypocercal tails have a longer lower lobe (e.g., flying fish). Protocercal tails extend around the vertebral column and are found in embryonic fish and hagfish. Diphycercal tails, seen in coelacanths and lungfish, are three-lobed, with vertebrae extending to the tail's end. Homocercal tails, common in most fish, are symmetrical, with no vertebrae extending into the lobes. These tails can be rounded, truncated, forked, emarginate (slightly inward-curved), or lunate (crescent-shaped). The anal fin is located on the ventral surface behind the anus and helps stabilize the fish while swimming. Paired pectoral fins, located on each side behind the operculum, are homologous to the forelimbs of tetrapods. In some fish, such as mudskippers and certain anglerfish, pectoral fins aid in walking. In species like sea robins and flying gurnards, certain rays of the pectoral fins are adapted into finger-like projections. The horns of manta rays are called cephalic fins, which are modifications of the anterior portion of the pectoral fins. Paired pelvic (ventral) fins are located below the pectoral fins and are homologous to the hindlimbs of tetrapods. These fins assist in vertical movement, sharp turns, and quick stops. In gobies, the pelvic fins are often fused into a single sucker disk, which can attach to objects. The adipose fin is a soft, fleshy fin found on the back behind the dorsal fin and just forward of the caudal fin. It is absent in many fish families but present in salmonids, characins, and catfish. Some fast-swimming fish have a horizontal caudal keel, a lateral ridge on the caudal peduncle that provides stability and support to the caudal fin. Finlets, small fins located behind the dorsal and anal fins, are found in some species like tuna and sauries. In many fish species, fins have evolved to facilitate internal fertilization. For example, the gonopodium is a modified anal fin in male live-bearing fish, used to impregnate females. It is movable and can account for up to 50% of the fish's body length in some species. Similar structures, such as the andropodium, are found in other fish families. Male cartilaginous fish have claspers, modified pelvic fins that channel semen into the female's cloaca during copulation. The skin of many fish is covered with scales, although some species have scutes (bony plates) or no outer covering at all (naked fish). Most fish are also covered in a protective layer of mucus. There are four main types of fish scales: Placoid scales (dermal denticles) resemble teeth and are made of dentin covered by enamel, typical of sharks and rays. Ganoid scales are flat, basal-looking scales with little overlap, found in gar and bichirs. Cycloid scales are small, oval-shaped scales with growth rings, seen in bowfin and remora. Ctenoid scales are similar to cycloid scales but have spines on one edge, as seen in halibut. Scutes are another type of scale, often modified into shield-like bony plates or ridged structures. Some fish, like pineconefish, are entirely or partially covered in scutes. Internally, the gas bladder (swim bladder) is an organ that helps fish control buoyancy, allowing them to maintain their depth without expending energy. It is absent in fast-swimming fish like tuna and mackerel. Certain fish have adaptations for hearing, such as the Weberian apparatus in Ostariophysians. Gills, located under the operculum, extract oxygen from water and expel carbon dioxide. In some species, such as the frilled shark, gills are externally visible. The labyrinth organ in Anabantoidei and Clariidae allows these fish to extract oxygen from the air. Gill rakers, bony projections on the gill arches, help filter feeders retain food particles. Electric fish can generate electric fields using modified muscles. Many fish species are hermaphroditic. Synchronous hermaphrodites possess both ovaries and testes simultaneously, while sequential hermaphrodites transition between genders during their lifetime.
